prompt: The requirement says a patient can cancel a booking online up to 24 hours before the session. The code does exactly that, and any patient can cancel anybody's booking. Where was the flaw born?

choices.text: In the implementation, because the code is where it shows
choices.why: It shows in the code, but the code did what the sentence asked. Nothing in the file contradicts the requirement.

choices.text: In the requirement
choices.why: Right. The sentence never says whose booking, and a missing sentence is a requirement flaw.

choices.text: In the design of the database
choices.why: The database stores who owns each booking perfectly well. Nobody asked the code to look.

choices.text: In the tests, which should have caught it
choices.why: Tests written from that sentence pass. They cannot ask for what the sentence never said.

prompt: The staff console was designed to answer from the internet, like the patient portal. Every line of its code is correct. Where is the flaw?

choices.text: In the implementation of the login form
choices.why: The login form may be perfect and the console is still exposed to everybody.

choices.text: Nowhere: correct code means a safe console
choices.why: Correct code inside a component placed in the wrong spot is still reachable by anyone.

choices.text: In the design: where the console sits
choices.why: Right. The shape of the system is the decision that went wrong, and no single file shows it.

choices.text: In the requirement for the agenda screen
choices.why: The agenda requirement says what the screen does. Where the console answers from is a design decision.

prompt: The design document says the patient search uses parameterised queries. The code joins the patient's text into the SQL string. Which reviewer is best placed to catch it, and when?

choices.text: The person who wrote the requirement, in the planning meeting
choices.why: The requirement was right. There is nothing in the planning meeting to find.

choices.text: A code reviewer or a test, before the change is merged
choices.why: Right. The code says something different from the design, so the code is where to look, and before merge is the cheapest moment.

choices.text: A threat model of the drawing
choices.why: The drawing already says parameterised. A threat model of it would find nothing wrong.

choices.text: Nobody, until a patient reports something odd
choices.why: That is the most expensive moment possible, and the flaw is visible long before it.

prompt: Match where a flaw was born to the review that catches it cheapest.

pairs.right: reading the story and asking who must not
a threat model of the drawing
a code review or a test

right_distractors: a scan of production after release

prompt: A reviewer reads the cancel function line by line and approves it. Later the missing ownership check is found. Why did the review not catch it?

choices.text: The reviewer was careless
choices.why: Care does not help: the file does what it was asked to do.

choices.text: Python hides that kind of check
choices.why: The language has nothing to do with it. The check was never written.

choices.text: Reviews only look at style, never at security
choices.why: A review can find security flaws; lesson 18 is about it. This flaw was not in the code to find.

choices.text: A line-by-line review compares code with what it was asked to do, and nobody asked for the check
choices.why: Right. A missing requirement is invisible from inside the code. It is found by asking who must not be able to do this.

prompt: The same missing sentence, found at three moments. Order them from the cheapest fix to the most expensive.
items: while reading the story in the planning meeting
by a failing test, before the change is merged
after release, when a patient's booking disappears

prompt: Why does this course name one language instead of writing its examples in pseudocode?

choices.text: The safe and unsafe calls differ by one comma
choices.why: Right. One comma and a pair of brackets separate the two queries, and pseudocode cannot show them.

choices.text: Python is the only language with parameterised queries
choices.why: Every mainstream language has them; the table maps them.

choices.text: Pseudocode would make the course longer and harder to translate
choices.why: Length is not the problem. Pseudocode hides the detail the lesson is about.

choices.text: Flaws exist only in Python programs
choices.why: The flaws and the defences are the same everywhere. Only the spelling changes.

prompt: Match each Python call to its equivalent in Go.
You move to a project in another framework. What does this course say to ask of its documentation first?

choices.text: Which version of Python it needs
choices.why: It may not be Python at all, and the version says nothing about defences.

choices.text: Which half of each defence it does without being asked
choices.why: Right. Flask escapes HTML and does not protect forms; another framework draws that line elsewhere, and you need to know where.

choices.text: Whether it has fewer known flaws than Flask
choices.why: A count of advisories does not tell you what you still have to write yourself.

choices.text: How to turn its defaults off for speed
choices.why: Turning off a default you have not understood is how a defence goes missing.

prompt: Why does every example in the course use invented patients and dates?

choices.text: Real patients' records are too large to fit in the memory of a small test program
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it; a handful of records fits anywhere.

choices.text: Flask refuses to store real names
choices.why: Flask stores whatever it is given.

choices.text: The portal holds health data, and real data must never be used to show a flaw
choices.why: Right. Health data is the most sensitive category under the LGPD, which is why the flaws matter and why nothing real is used.

choices.text: Invented data never contains flaws
choices.why: The flaws are in the code, not in the data.

prompt: Put the steps of every lesson's loop in order.
items: write the test that states the requirement
run it against the flawed code and watch it fail
change the code with the safe call
run the tests, watch them pass, commit both

prompt: Why does the course insist on watching the test fail before fixing the code?

choices.text: A test that never failed has not shown it reaches the flaw
choices.why: Right. The red run is the evidence that the test reaches the flaw. Without it, a green run proves nothing.

choices.text: pytest refuses to pass a test that has not failed first
choices.why: pytest has no memory of earlier runs.

choices.text: It is a tradition with no practical effect
choices.why: It has an effect: it shows the test can see the defect.

choices.text: The failure is what gets committed to git
choices.why: What gets committed is code and tests; the run's output is not committed.

prompt: Which of these stay within the rules of this course's lab? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: running the flawed application on 127.0.0.1 on your own laptop
choices.why: That is exactly the lab: your own application, reachable only from your machine.

choices.text: showing the flaw with one failing test, then fixing it
choices.why: That is the loop every lesson follows.

choices.text: pointing the same test at a friend's company website to see if it is vulnerable
choices.why: That is somebody else's system, without permission. It is outside the lab and, in Brazil, outside the law.

choices.text: starting the flawed application on 0.0.0.0 so a colleague can try it
choices.why: That puts a deliberately flawed program on the network, where anybody on it can reach it.

prompt: Why is installing on your own computer the recommended path for this course?

choices.text: It is the only path that runs Flask
choices.why: Flask runs in all three; the recommendation is about what needs isolating.

choices.text: Nothing here needs isolating: small programs of yours, listening only on 127.0.0.1
choices.why: Right. There is no malware and no target; the risk to manage is reachability, and 127.0.0.1 handles it.

choices.text: A virtual machine cannot run the web browser that lessons 7 to 9 need for the developer tools
choices.why: A virtual machine with a desktop runs a browser fine.

choices.text: Online environments forbid flawed code
choices.why: They do not; the caution there is about publishing a port.

prompt: The command that creates the course's isolated Python environment, followed by the folder's name, is: python3 -m ___
You do the course in an online development environment. Which setting matters most for these flawed applications?

choices.text: The amount of memory of the environment
choices.why: The applications are tiny; memory is not the risk.

choices.text: The colour theme of the editor
choices.why: Nothing to do with security.

choices.text: The region the environment runs in
choices.why: Where it runs matters less than who can reach it.

choices.text: Keeping its forwarded ports private
choices.why: Right. A public port publishes a deliberately flawed program to the internet.

prompt: pip installed Flask 3.1.3 and pytest 9.1.1. How many other packages did it install with them?
Why is each lesson's folder a git repository of its own?

choices.text: Flask refuses to start outside a repository
choices.why: Flask does not know or care about git.

choices.text: So that a fix is a readable diff
choices.why: Right. Commit the flawed version, fix, and git diff shows exactly what changed; and a broken experiment is one command from the version that worked.

choices.text: To publish each lesson on GitHub
choices.why: Nothing is published; these are local repositories.

choices.text: Because pytest only runs inside git
choices.why: pytest runs in any folder.

prompt: pytest prints `AssertionError: assert 200 == 404` for the last test. What happened?

choices.text: The booking 102 does not exist
choices.why: If it did not exist the answer would have been 404 and the test would pass.

choices.text: lucia cancelled rafael's booking
choices.why: Right. The app answered 200 where the test expected 404. That line is the flaw, shown by one request in your own application.

choices.text: The test is wrong: 200 means everything worked
choices.why: Everything worked for the wrong person. The test states what must be refused.

choices.text: The server was not running
choices.why: The test client needs no server; it answered, with 200.

prompt: Why is the clock a function of its own, `now()`, instead of calling `datetime.now()` inside the route?

choices.text: datetime.now() is not allowed inside Flask routes
choices.why: It is allowed; the reason is testing.

choices.text: It makes the application faster
choices.why: An extra function call makes nothing faster.

choices.text: So a test replaces it with monkeypatch and pins the date
choices.why: Right. The tests pin 1 November 2026 at 09:00, so the 24-hour rule is tested at a known moment.

choices.text: Because the server's clock is in another time zone
choices.why: Time zones are a real trap, but this function exists so tests can control time.

prompt: The fixture pins the clock with: monkeypatch.___(portal, "now", lambda: datetime(2026, 11, 1, 9, 0))
What does Flask's test client do that makes it right for these tests?

choices.text: It sends requests to the application without starting a server
choices.why: Right. The request goes through the same routes and checks, with no port and no network.

choices.text: It opens a headless browser and clicks the buttons on the page for you
choices.why: No browser is involved.

choices.text: It skips the checks in the route to save time
choices.why: It runs every check; that is the point.

choices.text: It only works when a server is already running on port 5000 of the same machine
choices.why: The tests ran with no server at all.

prompt: A colleague proposes a different fix: hide the cancel button on bookings that are not the patient's. What does the last test do with that change?

choices.text: It passes, because a patient who cannot see the button can no longer press it
choices.why: The test never saw a button; it sends the request directly.

choices.text: It still fails: the request is sent directly and the server still answers 200
choices.why: Right. Hiding a button changes the page, not what the server accepts. Lessons 3 and 12 come back to this.

choices.text: It errors, because the route was removed
choices.why: Nobody removed the route; only the button was hidden.

choices.text: It passes only in the browser
choices.why: pytest runs no browser; the result is the server's answer.

prompt: Why commit the flawed version before writing the fix?

choices.text: git refuses to record a fix with no earlier commit
choices.why: git records whatever you commit, first or not.

choices.text: To publish the flaw for others to study
choices.why: Nothing is published; the repository is on your machine.

choices.text: So git diff afterwards shows the fix and nothing else
choices.why: Right. The diff is one line, and a one-line diff is a review anybody can do.

choices.text: The tests read the previous commit to compare
choices.why: The tests read the code as it is now.

prompt: `python3 -c 'import flask'` prints `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'flask'`, and yesterday the lesson worked. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: The virtual environment is not active
choices.why: Right. A new terminal starts without it; the prompt has no (.venv).

choices.text: Flask was uninstalled overnight by an automatic system update
choices.why: Nothing uninstalls it. It lives in ~/sc/.venv.

choices.text: Python needs to be upgraded
choices.why: Python runs; it is looking in the wrong place for Flask.

choices.text: The app.py file has a syntax error in its first line
choices.why: The command imports flask, not app.py.

prompt: Match each message to its cause.

pairs.right: run from a folder with no app.py
another program is listening on port 5000
the virtual environment is not active

right_distractors: the firewall blocked the test client

prompt: On a Mac, `flask --app app run` reports that port 5000 is in use, though no other Flask is running. What is the likely holder, and a fix?

choices.text: pytest, which keeps the port after the tests
choices.why: The test client never opens a port.

choices.text: The browser, until you close every tab
choices.why: A browser connects to ports; it does not listen on 5000.

choices.text: The AirPlay Receiver; switch it off or use --port 5001
choices.why: Right. Since macOS 12 it listens on 5000.

choices.text: git, which uses port 5000 for commits
choices.why: A local commit touches no port.

prompt: A new story arrives: “a receptionist can export the agenda as a CSV file.” Which sentence is it missing?

choices.text: Which CSV library to use
choices.why: That is an implementation choice, not a missing requirement.

choices.text: Whose agenda: her own clinic's, or every clinic's
choices.why: Right. It is the cancel button again: the story says what, and never whose.

choices.text: What colour the export button is
choices.why: Nothing about security depends on it.

choices.text: How many rows the CSV file may hold before the export is split in two
choices.why: A detail of the format, not of who may export.

prompt: The reminder worker connects to the database with the owner's password, because that was the one that worked on the day it was written. Where was that flaw born?

choices.text: In the design: nobody decided what the worker should be allowed to do
choices.why: Right. The privileges of a component are a design decision, and here nobody made it.

choices.text: In the requirement for the reminder text
choices.why: The text of the message has nothing to do with the database account.

choices.text: In Python, which stores passwords badly
choices.why: The language is not the problem; the choice of account is.

choices.text: Nowhere: it works, so it is fine
choices.why: Working is the reason it was chosen, not evidence that it is safe.

prompt: Which of these are implementation flaws, rather than requirement or design flaws? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the search joins the patient's text into the SQL string
choices.why: The design said parameterised; the code said something else.

choices.text: the story never says whose booking may be cancelled
choices.why: A missing sentence is a requirement flaw.

choices.text: a template marks a patient's message as safe HTML
choices.why: A safe default switched off in one line of code.

choices.text: the staff console answers from the internet
choices.why: Where a component sits is a design decision.
